newsitem.title: CANADA: FOCUS-S&P raises Canadian debt rating outlook.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-S&P raises Canadian debt rating outlook.

text.p: Standard & Poor's said on Monday it upgraded Canada's foreign currency debt rating outlook because falling government deficits have put the country on better financial footing.
However, Canada still has too much debt to be reassigned the top triple-A rating it lost in 1992, the debt rating agency said.

New York-based S&P upgraded the outlook on Canada's foreign currency rating to stable from negative. The agency also confirmed the foreign currency debt rating at AA+ and the local currency debt rating at AAA.
Canada lost its AAA foreign currency rating in October, 1992 and the outlook was lowered to negative from stable in February, 1995.
In changing the outlook on the foreign currency debt rating, the agency said falling government deficits and reduced borrowing needs are providing the country with greater financial flexibility.

"The main reason (for the change in outlook) is the improved fiscal performance of the federal government, which has been quite successful in sticking to its deficit targets," said Valerie Blair, a director with Standard & Poor's in Toronto.
Canadian Finance Minister Paul Martin last week delivered a market-friendly federal budget which held the line on spending and committed the government to cutting the deficit for the next two years.
Blair said the budget added to the federal government's credibility on debt reduction.
Other factors which prompted the change in the rating outlook include a decline in reliance on foreign borrowing and reduced political uncertainty with regard to Quebec's sovereignty movement.
A high level of debt remains the main impediment to a full rating upgrade for Canada, S&P said.
The agency noted that the federal government's debt stood at about 75 percent of gross domestic product in fiscal 1996/97 ending March 31 and total government debt equalled about 100 percent of GDP.

"There has been no upgrade or even a positive outlook at this time because of the fact that Canada still has a very heavy debt burden," said Blair. While the agency does not have a specific debt-to-GDP target in mind for Canada, the ratio would have to be lower to earn a rating upgrade, Blair said.
Bond traders said the news had a positive impact on both bond and currency markets.
"It had an impact on the currency immediately," said Hank Cunningham, director of fixed-income with First Marathon Securities. "It's caused us to outperform the U.S. (bond market) as well."
